blocks.x: How Blockchain & Digital Trust lands in Capabilities — the constraints that shape the build, the gated delivery pattern, and the deltas we commit against your baseline.

In Insurance & Risk, blockchain & digital trust delivers distributed-ledger programs where a shared, verifiable record has economic value: enterprise dlt networks for multi-party workflows, asset tokenization, smart contract engineering and audit, provenance and traceability, decentralized identity with verifiable credentials, and on-chain analytics for compliance. That is the baseline pattern; the differentiator is what it connects to: enterprise dlt network engineering, asset tokenization & digital assets, smart contract engineering & audit — delivered on Dataq Ledger and Dataq Sentinel with the sector's regulatory posture built in.

items: Claims intake drowning in documents

FNOL packets, medical reports, repair estimates and police files arrive as unstructured documents; manual triage queues claims for days before an adjuster sees them. Leakage and customer patience both bleed in the queue.
Pricing sophistication outrunning governance

GLM-based pricing, telematics factors and external data enrichment multiply model complexity faster than validation capacity. Filings get challenged; model risk documentation is reconstructed under exam pressure.
Claims, policy and exposure data fragmented
Underwriting, claims and finance each hold their own truth; loss triangles reconcile by spreadsheet. Portfolio analytics that should steer the cycle take months of manual assembly.

blocks.x: Two regimes anchor the control design here: Solvency II / NAIC RBC regimes and DORA (for EU insurers). ICT third-party and resilience obligations like banking peers. Evidence for both is generated by the delivery itself — control tests, replay trails and documentation are artifacts of the program, not a reconstruction project.

The weekly rhythm below is identical across programs of this type. Weeks 1–2 are measurement only: we lock the current metric with your team and both sides sign it before a line of build starts. Weeks 3–8 deliver a bounded pilot — one decision path, one workflow, one plant or one portfolio — with a named control owner on your side. Weeks 9–12 turn what worked into runbooks, monitoring and enablement, then report the measured delta against the baseline. A missed gate means a documented stop-or-redirect decision, not a quiet extension.
